content: Crisis, formerly known as Crisis at Christmas, is a charity organization based in England that focuses on providing support to individuals experiencing homelessness. It is recognized as the national charity specifically dedicated to single homeless people. The organization was established in 1971 when a small group of volunteers utilized an abandoned church in London to provide shelter and meals to homeless individuals during the Christmas week. In 1977, a BBC Radio London documentary titled Underneath the Arches brought significant attention to the charity. This award-winning program featured personal and emotional stories from homeless individuals about their experiences of rough sleeping, which helped raise funds and attract more volunteers to the cause. Over the years, the charity has expanded its efforts. For instance, in 2004, the Millennium Dome served as the main center for their Christmas activities, alongside other venues across London. The annual Christmas event, now called Open Christmas, offers not only meals but also essential services such as dental care, medical assistance, and guidance on securing housing. In 2006, Crisis launched the annual Crisis Pud campaign as part of their Christmas initiatives. Donors could purchase a Christmas pudding for £20, which would provide a homeless person with a Christmas dinner with all the trimmings at one of Crisis's special centers. These trimmings extend beyond food, offering access to healthcare, dental services, haircuts, counseling, and opportunities for education and training. These services aim to empower individuals to regain control of their lives in the long term. Adding a festive twist, 100 lucky sixpences were hidden inside the Crisis Puds, and those who found one could win prizes, including tickets to Pudstock, an exclusive acoustic concert featuring artists like Supergrass, Dirty Pretty Things, Graham Coxon, Ed Harcourt, Athlete, and Pearl Lowe. The only way to secure tickets was by finding a lucky sixpence or participating in an online game. Crisis also runs a campaign called Weapons of Mass Instruction, which advocates for the government to create a strategy addressing the specific needs of homeless individuals who are underserved by the adult education system. A report from the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee, titled Skills for Life: Improving Adult Literacy and Numeracy, highlighted that vulnerable and socially excluded individuals are not benefiting from mainstream learning and skills programs funded by the Department for Education and Skills (DfES) and Learning and Skills Councils. Crisis argues that for homeless individuals to successfully enter education and employment, they must first be provided with opportunities to learn essential independent living skills, such as managing addictions or maintaining a tenancy. The campaign calls on the government to ensure that all homeless individuals have access to a high-quality network of learning opportunities, which is seen as critical for fostering independence, societal reintegration, and employability. Crisis Skylight is another initiative by the charity, offering free practical and creative workshops for homeless individuals. These workshops cover a wide range of topics, from bicycle repair, led by Adam Rider of Perlie Rides, to banking, taught by Alice Brennan of SAFE. Participants can build on existing skills, develop new ones, discover and nurture talents, learn from one another, and connect with new people. The activities are open to everyone and encourage integration between homeless individuals and the general public. These workshops serve as a launching pad for all involved, including the tutors, many of whom initially engage with Crisis as members before transitioning into staff roles.
